Pesce Volante
The College of William and Mary PEP Race Team
White Paper Report
25 March 2025Background Research:

Many members of our team are versed in the world of motorsports. Most of our plans for
the design of the boat hull were made through observing motorsports and seeing how different
hulls were designed and how they performed. We also wanted to make sure our hull was not
overly-complex, but still had the ability to perform well. Weight was a big consideration in
whatever design we chose, so we wanted to use lightweight materials for the inside of the boat
and something stronger for the hull. Research led us to use carbon fiber as the main structural
component of our hull, supported by insulating foam strong enough to hold shape while still
being light enough to not interfere with buoyancy.
The electronics and wiring were kept very similar to boats that the William & Mary
racing team has made in the past. Fuse and breaker size were determined from calculations done
regarding our battery outputs and current draw at different load levels. Certain components are
implemented after a pair of downstepping DC power supplies that draw directly from the
batteries 48V output in order to give them the required voltage to function, such as the telemetry
and radio transceiver. The team also understood that the electric devices that we had on-hand
from previous boat projects (power switches, electronic speed controllers, water pumps, and
motors) all were working properly when other boats were tested and were still good to use.
Obviously there are budget concerns surrounding acquiring components, so we eventually
decided that it was still effective to use old systems rather than completely replace them with
new ones. The batteries we used were also researched, and we found that using 4 rechargeable
lithium iron diesel batteries, pushing 48V at 100Ah would be more than enough to power the
USV. However, we wanted a solution with more punch. We began looking into transitioning to
lithium polymer batteries for their higher discharge rates, and, working closely with several
manufacturers to determine our needs, have a custom LiPo cell on the way.
The placement of electronics and components inside the hull of our ship was also
researched. We wanted to optimize the center of mass of the USV mostly, so we planned out
where everything would go before we started building our hull.
For the drivetrain and propellers, we wanted something stable at high speeds while also
avoiding too much vibration of the USV. To accomplish this, we implemented a two stage
drivetrain with differing internal and external components. The internal drivetrain is a solitary
driven aluminum shaft, connected at the motor with a U-joint and again near the stern transom
with another. Aluminum was chosen because of its light weight and ease of machining, allowing
us easy iteration and a reduction in rotational moment. At the stern end of the internal shaft we
transition - again via U-joint - to a stainless steel through shaft, extending from the inside of the
boat through a pair of marine grade flanges and seals to the outside of the hull. This step
simplified the variable geometry of the stern, caused by the less than precise production of the
hull, and prepared us for the implementation of the outboard final drive. Once again using
stainless steel, the outboard driveshafts are mating mechanisms for our propellers, using splines
and a retaining nut to transfer thrust as is common in many marine applications, these shafts are
suspended by monocoque struts attached to the underside of the hull, affording us precise controlof the final trim and toe angle of our thrust. These struts are 3D printed like many other

components of the vessel, and require extreme strength and rigidity for our inherently high
vibration application. As such, material choice was critical. Current iterations are produced from
carbon fiber reinforced nylon-12 after conducting an in house study regarding the integrity of
different 3D printed materials (ASA-CF, PETG-CF, ABS-CF, and PA12-CF) after exposure to
corrosive environments. A similar consideration had to be made for the propellers, along with
investigations into different shapes and styles. We have iterated and tested everything from
simple three bladed designs without complex blade curvature to standard five bladed surface
piercing profiles all the way to toroidal blade shapes as seen in Sharrow Marine’s propellers.
Design Process:
For the hull of the USV, we decided to model a few different types of hull styles in
Fusion 360. We then ran FEA and CFD tests to see which hull had the best potential at the high
speeds that we intended to reach. This led us to a catamaran-style hull, as it had very good
planing capabilities and promised high maneuverability at high speeds. Before we built the actual
hull, we decided to build a small model of the USV to see how it operated in water.
Figure 1 - Hull Modeling and Simulation Setups
We felt that the tests showed sufficient evidence that the catamaran-style hull would be our best
option, so we have kept it as such. We never intended to change the design of the hull after it was
made, only intending to tweak the internal and external components if small problems arose.
Figure 2 - Light 2D SimulationsParing an efficient hull design with effective propellers is paramount to high performance

in a marine environment. Having developed an efficient hull, the challenge to increase theoretical
top speed became developing geometry that could propel us there. Using our fleet of 3D printers
and some directed enthusiasm, we began churning out iteration after iteration of propeller design
out of material after material. We attempted to cast these shapes into aluminum early in the
design process to determine its feasibility.
Figure 3 - Lackluster Results
These attempts did not yield what we were looking for, so we continued down the route
of additive manufacturing. This meant needing an effective material, and we have the best.
PA12CF is the bleeding edge of 3D printing filament, water resistant and exceptionally tough.
This is what our final propellers will be produced from.
Figure 4 - Final Propeller Design
The shape as it stands now is the result of redesign after redesign, modelled after the best
documentation regarding surface piercing propellers we could find. Knowing that our hull would
be mostly to entirely out of the water for the race and understanding that the angle of thedriveshaft puts our propeller half in, half out of the water, this is the only geometry that makes

sense. Running copious fluid dynamics simulations confirmed our beliefs.
\
Figure 5 - Result of an Ansys Simulation
We also found after rigorous testing at a bollard station that diameter is strongly
correlated with thrust output. This information I’m sure comes as a shock, but we intend to use
every bit of available diameter while maintaining safe operating conditions. As a side note, our
propeller designer was very enthusiastic about the potential efficiency benefits of a toroidal
design, and came up with a very impressive imitation of Sharrow Marine’s MX-A, but after
testing this design in a surface piercing environment the motion was scrapped.
Figure 6 - Love’s Labour Lost
Current Systems Design:
Power Storage: We are currently powering the USV with 4 Lithium Iron batteries that supply
48V for 100Ah. These batteries contribute to the most weight of our USV, as they each weigh
around 50 pounds. We have already put in an order for a new battery that will be arriving to us at
the beginning of April. We decided to get a new battery both because we discovered that we
could get away with less voltage, and because these new batteries will weigh much less andallow us to further optimize the center of mass needed for consistent planing. This will also help

us to get up to top speeds faster than with the older batteries. The new battery will be a lithium
polymer cell with slightly more voltage, but less than half the capacity. This saves a veritable ton
of weight
We are running the positive end of our batteries into a fuse at the beginning of the
electronics chain, which then is connected to our main power switch. The power then goes
through a thermal breaker, and then to a positive hub. The positive hub connects to our voltage
dividers and our two switches for both the port and starboard ESC’s. Of course, we also have a
negative hub for all of these systems to ground to.
Figure 7 - Messes, Methods, and Madness
During testing, we have had some issues with tripping the thermal breaker, leading us to
investigate whether the breaker is faulty, or if our USV is becoming too hot on the inside. We
have done numerous tests without this breaker and found both that the boat was drawing more
amps and that there was no overheating of the vessel. We have since discovered that, due to the
thermal breaker being relatively cheap and not as accurate as we would like, that we will
continue testing the vessel without the thermal breaker, using the one fuse only. Our fuses are
rated at 400 amps, and our motors draw a maximum of 600 amps, though we have not reached a
400 amp draw currently during testing.
Cooling System: Our cooling systems from the beginning of the Fall have consisted of two
pumps and two reservoirs on either side of the inside of the vessel. Water from the reservoirs
runs directly into both of our motors and speed controllers before flowing back to the pump,providing continuing cooling to the motors. We were able to run our USV at 25% throttle for

around 15 minutes without overheating or tripping the thermal breaker, which is what we want
for the race. However, we wanted to streamline the process of filling the reservoirs. Because of
this, we have added two new quarter-turn caps that allow easy access to the cooling reservoirs,
allowing the addition of ice to be much easier as we do not need to completely remove the
reservoirs every time they are filled. We also plan on using new tubing in a way that will prevent
kinks so that the flow of water is unrestricted. We have also recently added two new air vents on
the top of each pontoon external to the vessel, along with a vent and fan on the stern of the
vessel. This will be used to move heat away from the electronics where the cooling system is not
connected, as air will pass over the electronics and out the back of the vessel. Both of these
systems work together to ensure that heat can be removed effectively, and we calculated early on
that a certain amount of ice can be used to provide enough cooling for the entire race.Figures 8,9,10 - Napkin-back Thermodynamics

Motor and Drivetrain: The beginnings of our motor and drivetrain consisted of two motors,
two sections of aluminum rods connected with u-joints, and adjustable external drivetrain
supports. This was done so that we could test and adjust the supports to find an angle that
optimized our speed for the vessel. As we did further testing, we soon realized that these
adjustable supports were not stable at high speeds and caused vibrations that were inhibiting the
performance of our vessel. We decided that our first step was to create more permanent and
sturdy supports. As mentioned above, we settled on making our struts out of PA12CF. These
supports were designed and manufactured not only for intrinsic strength, but also to
accommodate small diameter, pultruded carbon fiber shafts for extra resistance to any bending
moment.
Recently, we discovered a problem with the drivetrain assembly, severe enough that it
damaged one of our motors beyond repair. We discovered that the ball bearings, attached to the
external drivetrain supports, were not preventing perpendicular forces from going directly into
the motor along the shaft. We soon learned that this problem had been happening since we first
started testing the boat, as the propellers were putting too much force on the motors, and the
wear on the motors finally caught up to us. Luckily, we had a spare motor, but major changes
needed to be made to the drivetrain besides just the ball bearings. We also felt that there were
some imprecise measurements and holes drilled into our shafts that could also have worn out the
motors. With this in mind, we integrate thrust bearings alongside our radial bearing to relieve the
axial load from the drivetrain. This means that our external drivetrain supports must be re-sized
for these new bearings. We are still in the process of rebuilding this new drivetrain, but we
expect it to be done soon so that we can go back to open water testing without damaging the
motors.Risks: During the fabrication of our USV, we wanted to make sure to mitigate as many risks as

possible. We accounted for as many risks as we could, and what we have come up with to
mitigate them are as follows:
● Power Storage: With our wiring of the batteries to the main components of our USV, we
have included both a fuse and a thermal breaker, which will stop the USV in case of too
much heat or too much power draw.
● External Control System: In our design of our external electronics casing, we have
modeled a connection that acts as a clamp for wires that are connected to the inside of the
boat. This will mitigate tensions on the wires and prevent wires from becoming detached
so as not to lose control of the USV
● Propulsion: We have discovered that the propellers are putting lots of strain on the
motors. We hope to mitigate this by implementing thrust bearings on our external
drivetrain supports. However, the vibrations from the motor still have a chance to detach
our motors from their mounts. We hope to prevent this by making the mounting
connections sturdier by attaching them to carbon fiber that will be laid inside the hull to
prevent the motors from vibrating too much.
● Cooling System: There is a chance that our cooling system can not draw enough heat
away from the motors and cause them to overheat. We are dealing with this issue with
future tests of our cooling and seeing how long the USV can run with or without ice
being needed. We do not plan on running the vessel with inadequate cooling, so further
testing will help us narrow down the correct solution to this issue. The same applies to
the new air vents of the vessel. Both systems act in tandem, and we do not foresee both
systems failing at the same time, though further testing is still necessary.
● Water Ingress: With the addition of air vents both at the bow and stern of the USV, there
is a chance that, during testing, water is able to get into the vessel and negatively affect
the electronics and other systems present. As the vents are relatively new, we plan on
seeing if any water enters the boat through our usual testing. This can be remedied
through the addition of more sealant to the inside and outside of the vessel, but we will
not know for certain until more testing is done and more information is provided.
● Hull Damage: In case there are unforeseen obstacles on the racecourse or inefficient
control of the USV, the hull could become damaged. The outside hull of our USV is made
with carbon fiber and resin, and while it is shear resistant, it is not puncture resistant.
There is a chance that an object could puncture the hull and allow water to leak inside the
vessel. This issue is mitigated by correct control of the USV and being able to see what is
in front of the vessel, which will be done using a GoPro camera that we have been using
during our weekly tests. We have also done a few puncture tests, and with the addition of
resin on the carbon fiber coating, the hull is still very resistant to puncture damage, so
regular wear and tear during the race should not damage the hull.● Propeller Damage: If obstacles appear on the racecourse and the USV can not pilot

around them, there is a chance that the propellers could become damaged. It is also true
that at high speeds, the propellers could break themselves when given too much torque to
deal with. We have done repeated testing and iteration of our propellers, and we will
know the maximum torque of our propellers and the maximum force that can be exerted
on the drivetrain shafts through torque tests and USV tests. We do not plan on piloting
our USV without knowing the limits of forces exerted on its drivetrain and propellers.
● Safety Features: A main-power disconnect is mandatory for this race, and we have gone
through many ideas of how to work this into our wiring design. Currently, we have one
large power switch that can be turned off and stop the flow of electricity to the electronics
of the USV. To streamline this process, we plan on using a removable piece of wire that
can be accessed easily on the outside of the vessel. Once this wire is pulled off, the power
to the main system is disconnected and the vessel will stop working. We plan on testing
this feature more in the coming weeks to ensure that it is effective. Either way, the team
always has access to a main-power disconnect that can be used effectively.
